frameworks.claim: Thermal constraints limit the performance and reliability of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in compute systems.
frameworks.mechanism: The base die of an HBM cube, which performs the most complex work, generates the most heat. This heat can lead to reliability issues with DRAM refreshes, necessitating architectural solutions that prioritize thermal management over performance optimizations.
frameworks.boundary: This reasoning is based on the specific limitations of HBM technology and the thermal challenges it faces, as evidenced by the author's observations on heat extraction and die temperature.

evidence.quote: “Compute is scaling at roughly 3x every 2 years. HBM, while it has solved a lot of the bandwidth issues and scaled up bandwidth, is lagging and is more like 2x every 2 years. So the memory wall is still present, and in fact, it may be getting worse.”

“If you think of an HBM cube, the heat is getting extracted at the top. The base die is typically the hottest part of the die, because it’s doing some of the most complex work. … DRAM doesn’t like to be hot. So refreshes of DRAM start to become a problem for reliability if it gets too hot. Figuring out what the thermal solutions are is very, very critical, and it’s getting to the point where we are now architecting solutions around thermals instead of the other way around.” — Raghu Sreeramaneni
